Development guide

Product discovery

Decide which problem to solve, test possible solutions and use the evidence to choose what to build.

Product discovery combines research, comparison of user needs and testing of possible solutions. Use this guide’s six steps to plan that work with Product, Design and Engineering. A fictional service-desk example follows the evidence from an initial problem to a decision to implement a limited pilot.

  • Updated: 28 October 2026
On this page
Start together The learning journey 1. Understand the problem Research plan Technical discovery 2. Define value and explore alternatives 3. Design the experiment Experiment methods 4. Prototype and learn 5. Evaluate and decide 6. Prepare the handoff Optional deep dives Sources

Start together: Product, Design and Engineering

Name the people responsible for Product, Design and Engineering at the start. Together, they choose what to investigate, review the findings and recommend the next investment. Name the person authorised to make that decision.

Keep AI assistance connected to evidence

Give each AI-assisted task a question, permitted inputs, an expected output and a reviewer. When an AI agent uses tools to carry out several steps, set its permissions before it starts. Label observations, AI interpretations and untested suggestions separately. The reviewer checks the original sources before using a generated claim to support a decision.

Related reading: Product School’s AI discovery guide [15]. The checks in this guide are recommendations. NIST’s Generative AI Profile [17], action MS-2.5-003 and Appendix A.1.6, support checking generated citations and retaining content provenance.

Agree the outcome, experience and technical questions

Product defines the intended outcome, Design examines the user’s experience, and Engineering investigates whether the solution can work. Any of them can initiate discovery. They test the proposal together, with research, testing, operations, security and other specialists as needed.

Record the problem, proposed solution and open questions in a concept brief. Develop a product requirements document (PRD) as the intended behaviour becomes clearer. Link both to the experiment record and decision.

Inspiration: Sheth’s “3-in-a-Box” proposal [5] connects intent, interaction and implementation. It is practitioner advice; the working approach here is this guide’s recommendation.

For each experiment, choose the assumption most likely to invalidate the proposal. Inspect the same prototype and observations, then update the design, technical approach and PRD together.

Record disagreements about scope, investment or risk and refer unresolved choices to the decision owner. Involve the specialists and approvers required by the decision.

Reference: human judgement and agent-supported work

Use the table to agree responsibilities and decision owners across the team. One person may cover several disciplines.

Human judgement and agent-supported work
ParticipantHuman judgement and accountabilityAgent-supported work
ProductProblem, outcomes, priorities, trade-offs and proposed solutionResearch summaries, options, draft specifications and decision evidence
DesignUser behaviour, desirability, usability and interaction principlesConcept variants, prototypes, journey analysis and heuristic checks
Engineering and architectureFeasibility, architecture, reversibility, security and operational qualityCode exploration, technical spikes, plans, tests and dependency analysis
AI and dataData quality, model behaviour, evaluation design and runtime controlsDataset analysis, evaluations, tracing and model comparison
Risk and compliancePolicy interpretation, thresholds, exceptions and accountable acceptanceContinuous checks, evidence collection, control mapping and risk screening
AgentsNo organisational accountabilityResearch, challenge, specification drafting, prototyping, testing and evaluation

For this to work, the shared environment needs:

  • access to current, relevant product and technical context;
  • clear ownership, permissions and decision authority;
  • visible agent activity, sources, outputs and status;
  • a structured route for review, feedback and exceptions; and
  • explicit human approval for high-consequence decisions.

People remain accountable for delegated work. Review technical limits alongside user needs before investing in a solution.

Read about human–agent team composition.

Source: [1], “Structure the team right”, on named accountability and multidisciplinary teams. The agent responsibilities and working environment above are this guide’s recommendations.

Follow the evidence through four phases

Product discovery asks whether a problem is worth solving and whether a proposed solution earns further investment. In the AI-Software Development Lifecycle (AI-SDLC), implementation turns that intent into verified software and returns new learning.

When to enter or revisit discovery

Start with a user or business problem, an obligation, or a new capability whose value is uncertain. Bring existing observations, alternatives and constraints, and name the person responsible for collecting evidence. Return to discovery when research, incidents or delivery findings challenge the intended outcome. Send well-understood defects directly to implementation.

This is a recommended learning sequence, not a new set of organisational approval gates. Scale the evidence to the consequences of the decision.

Business discovery investigates need, value, adoption and affordability. Technical discovery investigates whether a candidate solution can work within delivery and operating limits. Carry both through every phase; a critical technical question can justify a test before the problem framing is complete.

Develop the brief and PRD as you learn

One evolving product intent, with increasing evidence
ArtefactPurpose and maturity
Concept brief (Frame)Why this user, problem and possible direction deserve investigation. Includes alternatives, baseline, assumptions and the next test; it is not an implementation-ready specification.
Draft PRD (Test)A PRD describing proposed behaviour, interaction states, constraints and provisional acceptance criteria: observable results the product should demonstrate. Link tests to the version they examine and revise the draft as findings change intent.
Evidence-backed PRD (Handoff)Versioned scope with linked evidence, user interface (UI) designs or application programming interface (API) examples, testable criteria and owners for open questions. It remains revisable; commitment is not production approval.

AI-assisted development uses AI to help research, draft, build or check software. An AI product uses AI at runtime; only products with agents taking or choosing actions need the optional agent-journey checks. People retain accountability in every case.

Follow one fictional example: a service-desk knowledge assistant for staff answering routine access questions. Expand the example in each step to follow its evidence and artefacts. Every number, identifier, threshold and result is illustrative, not an EDS policy or a measured organisational result.

ProblemValueExperimentLearningDecisionHandoff

1. Understand the problem

Learn whose task is failing, where the difficulty occurs and why it matters before choosing a solution. Observe the workflow, speak with affected people and examine support or operational records. Separate observations from hypotheses: proposed explanations or expected results that still need testing.

Use 6W to investigate and 4C to check the statement

Use the Defence Product Playbook’s six questions (6W) [1] to draft the problem statement: what goes wrong, where, when, who is affected, why it happens and why it matters. Include how often the problem occurs. Then apply its four checks (4C) below.

The 4C problem-statement check, adapted from the Defence Product Playbook
CriterionWhat the statement shows
ClarityOne user group, the task they attempt, the friction, and how severe and frequent it is
ConsequenceThe quantified cost if the problem stays unsolved
CauseA theory of change: how the problem arises and where a change could improve the outcome
ConfirmationEvidence that supports the identified cause

The playbook warns against four weak substitutes for a problem: an aspiration, a proposed solution, an end-of-life notice or a vague complaint. Explain who is affected and what happens if nothing changes. For an ageing system, describe foreseeable support, security or recovery problems with dates and evidence. You can plan migration before users experience a failure.

To compare discretionary improvements, assess severity, frequency and reach (SFR): how serious the problem is, how often it occurs and how many people it affects. Score each low, medium or high, with evidence and uncertainty. Use the scores to inform the decision.

Consider mandatory obligations and unacceptable risks before ranking discretionary work. A rare problem may still demand action because of serious harm, security exposure, an accessibility barrier or failure of an essential service. Record the reason, urgency and decision owner.

Plan research around the next decision

Agree which decision the research will inform, what could change it and how much time and money to spend. For each question, name a source, method and owner. Review existing findings first, and recruit people with different tasks, experience and access needs.

  • Problem evidence: observe the current task and alternatives; record friction, consequences and exceptions with the source and date.
  • Starting measure (baseline): record the current outcome, how it is measured and who would benefit from improvement. Record gaps that prevent a credible comparison.
  • System context: ask system owners to demonstrate the relevant interfaces, permissions and failure behaviour. Mark unconfirmed capabilities as assumptions.
  • Findings: separate observations from explanations, retain contradictions and identify the next question. Decide whether the evidence supports comparing opportunities or requires further investigation.

Problem research follows the Design Council’s Discover and Define [2]. The decision record and system checks are this handbook’s recommended practices.

Check AI summaries against the research

Link each theme in an AI summary to source passages or timestamps, collection dates and user groups. A reviewer checks the surrounding context, including contradictory observations. Review recordings or observation notes when transcripts omit relevant behaviour.

Remove duplicate records before counting participants or events. Compare equivalent periods and channels, noting changes in who supplied the data. Check a separate sample of source records for issues the summary missed, including rare but serious problems.

Use the checked findings to choose the next study or technical test and name its owner. Confirm generated technical explanations with system owners, current documentation or executable checks. Review findings when new evidence could change the decision.

Test feasibility alongside user value

Use SVPG’s feasibility risk [3] to ask whether the available people, time and technology can deliver a candidate solution. Engineering leads the investigation with Product, Design and the affected service owners. The following checklist is a handbook recommendation, scaled to the proposed scope.

Technical assumptions to resolve before a bounded commitment
AssumptionCheck and retained evidence
The critical path can workCheck and retained evidenceCompare reuse, purchase and build options. Exercise the uncertain interface or capability; retain executable results, versions, dependency owners and untested conditions.
Data and actions are permittedCheck and retained evidenceTest identity, data access and action boundaries with representative permitted and denied cases. Record missing access and decisions needed from accountable owners.
The service can meet operating limitsCheck and retained evidenceMeasure relevant latency, volume, failure and recovery behaviour. State test conditions, quality targets and differences from the intended environment.
Delivery and operation are affordableCheck and retained evidenceEstimate build, integration, migration, support and exit costs as ranges. Confirm skills, capacity and external lead times; record assumptions and sensitivity.
AI adds useful capability, where proposedCheck and retained evidenceCompare the AI with a simpler approach on representative cases kept separate from development and tuning. Retain model, prompt and data versions, failure cases, human correction effort and cost per successful task.

If an important technical question remains open, run a short investigation, often called a spike. Agree its question, owner, test environment, success criteria and budget. Report what ran, what failed and what remains unknown. A simulated integration tests the interaction; test the real dependency separately and carry findings into the technical requirements document (TRD).

Fictional service-desk example 1 of 6: understand the problem

Problem record P-1: staff answering routine access questions repeatedly search for the right knowledge article. In 24 fictional observed cases over two weeks, median handling time is 12 minutes; seven cases need a colleague’s help locating an article.

6W: what: slow guidance; where: the service desk; when: routine access queries; who: desk staff; why: retrieval may be difficult; why it matters: staff effort and user waiting. The sample shows friction; poor retrieval is still a causal hypothesis.

4C: clarity names the task and group; consequence is time and waiting; cause is the retrieval hypothesis; confirmation is incomplete. Check article accuracy and observe search behaviour before attributing the delay to retrieval alone.

Follow the example: 2 of 6.

Output: An evidenced problem statement, source notes, affected users and unresolved causes. Next: Use step 2 to compare ways of changing the outcome.

2. Define value and explore alternatives

Compare the current workflow with process changes, clearer content, conventional software and AI options. Define the intended improvement before refining the interface. When starting with a new technology, investigate which user problem it could solve.

An opportunity is a user need, pain point or desire that could contribute to a desired outcome when addressed. A concept is one possible response. Keep the outcome, opportunity and solution distinct so the team can reject a solution without losing the underlying need. See Teresa Torres’s definitions [8].

Turn research into an opportunity shortlist

  1. Group findings by need and cause. Trace each opportunity to affected users, the task, observed friction or foreseeable risk, and its consequence. Identify where a change could improve the outcome.
  2. Write an opportunity record. Capture evidence and confidence, baseline, expected value, strategic fit, urgency, enabling capabilities, dependencies and the highest-risk assumptions.
  3. Compare opportunities jointly. Product, Design and Engineering weigh reach, severity, frequency, inclusion, expected benefit, feasibility, lifetime cost and dependency risk. Record uncertainty and the reason for the ranking.
  4. Choose the next learning investment. Select opportunities to investigate or validate, record deferred and rejected ones with reasons, and assign an owner and review trigger. A high-value but uncertain opportunity can justify a small feasibility experiment.

Use scores to make assumptions visible, rather than to manufacture precision. Keep mandatory obligations and intolerable risks explicit when they override discretionary priorities. Revisit the shortlist when new capabilities, constraints or evidence change the available choices.

Check the assumptions behind priorities

Compare planned investment with actual effort, measured outcomes, obligations and dependencies. Use competitor research to suggest questions for users; a supplier’s launch announcement alone does not show what customers need.

Compare delivering sooner with testing the largest uncertainty first. Use the same intended outcomes and resource limits for both plans. Engineering checks dependencies, quality targets, operating cost and how easily the approach could change. Record what evidence would change the order of work.

For an AI-generated ranking, record the benefit, effort and dependency assumptions. Check whether plausible changes would reverse the ranking. Agreement across generated answers does not replace evidence.

Choose the starting measure, target and limits

Choose the main outcome measure and record its baseline: the current value, people or cases covered, period and collection method. Agree a target before testing. Set guardrails: limits on errors, security, privacy, accessibility, reliability, cost and review effort that the experiment needs to respect.

Assess access restrictions separately from average quality scores. An accurate answer still fails the test if it exposes restricted information. Finding no failures in a small test does not prove that failures are impossible.

Measurement thread: baseline → target and guardrails → experiment result → decision. Set the first two here; preserve them alongside later results.

Write a short concept brief

Before committing to delivery, write a concept brief explaining the problem, proposed solution and reasons to test it. Aim for one page with evidence links. Anyone in Product, Design or Engineering can draft it; the three refine it together.

The following is a suggested working format. Record:

  • User, problem and evidence: the target user, their task, the consequence of doing nothing, and linked observations, requests or analysis. Distinguish a request from evidence of its underlying need.
  • Outcome and value: the outcome the user needs, the value to the organisation and why the opportunity matters now.
  • Proposed direction and alternatives: the initial solution hypothesis, the expected interaction and the alternatives worth comparing.
  • Feasibility and boundaries: enabling capabilities, known constraints, exclusions, risks, dependencies and unresolved assumptions.
  • Reasons to change or stop: evidence or limits, agreed in advance, that would trigger a redesign, a pivot or a stop.

Name the brief’s owner, next experiment and decision owner. Share it with relevant stakeholders before seeking the next investment, then update it as evidence changes. Develop a draft PRD from this brief as the intended behaviour becomes clearer. Label assumptions and provisional criteria explicitly.

Use AI differently when widening and narrowing

  • When widening, use AI to research broadly, summarise evidence, generate different concepts, surface hidden assumptions and explore alternative journeys or technical approaches.
  • When narrowing, compare options against user value, strength of evidence, feasibility, cost, risk and strategic fit. Do not choose an option because it is the most polished or the easiest to generate.

Keep source links beside research summaries and check them before using a claim. Treat generated personas, synthetic interviews and an agent’s critique as prompts for research, not observations of real users.

Challenge the proposal before refining it

AI can turn a stakeholder request into a polished specification quickly. That speed creates a risk: refining an idea nobody has challenged. Before commitment, ask a reviewer, or an agent instructed to act as a critic, to work through these questions:

  1. What evidence shows that the problem is important and severe enough?
  2. What happens if the organisation does nothing?
  3. Which users experience the problem, and which do not?
  4. Why this solution rather than a materially different one?
  5. Which assumption could invalidate the proposal?
  6. What is the cheapest credible experiment that could disprove it?
  7. Which requirements conflict, and what fails at much greater scale?

This challenge complements user research and domain expertise; it does not replace them. Regulated, safety-critical, legally consequential and highly specialised questions still need qualified human reviewers.

Fictional service-desk example 2 of 6: define value and explore alternatives

Concept brief v0.1: compare a curated article index, clearer guidance and a draft-response assistant. The assistant is a hypothesis, not the predetermined answer. It only retrieves permitted articles and drafts advice; staff review it, and it cannot grant access or submit requests.

Baseline → target: 12-minute median → at most 9 minutes on comparable tasks, including checking and correction. Also seek at least 7 of 8 staff completing correctly without help, with no restricted content exposed in the tested cases. These exploratory thresholds guide the next investment, not a production release.

Product owns the outcome and cost case; Design owns the task and review journey; Engineering investigates retrieval and permissions. The theory of change is that easier source retrieval reduces search and checking effort without weakening correctness.

Follow the example: 3 of 6.

Output: Concept brief, alternatives, testable assumptions, baseline, target and guardrails. Next: Choose the highest unresolved risk and write the experiment before building.

3. Design the experiment

Draft the PRD from the concept brief before prototyping. Describe proposed behaviour, interaction states, constraints and provisional acceptance criteria. Link the experiment to that version and revise the draft as you learn.

Ask what evidence could change the team’s mind. Product, Design and Engineering select the greatest unresolved risk together. Use a sketch when it can answer the question; use working integration only when that is needed for credible evidence.

Write an experiment record

The following is a suggested working record. Complete it before building or testing so the result can inform a decision:

  1. State the assumption. Name the user, task and behaviour expected to change. Record the current outcome as a baseline.
  2. Choose the evidence. Record the method, participants or data, prototype version and conditions. Link the experiment safety check, including permissions and stop conditions. Include relevant access needs and users likely to struggle.
  3. Set the decision rule. Agree a success measure, failure limits and a time or cost budget. Name the reviewer and next decision.
  4. Record observations and limits. Keep results linked to source notes. Separate what happened from the team’s interpretation, and record missing or contradictory evidence.

Choose a method that answers the question

Use interviews to investigate needs, prototypes to test interactions and technical investigations to check capabilities. To test whether a change caused an improvement, plan a comparison that accounts for other explanations. Choose a starting point from Figure 5, or open the method reference below.

Reference: compare twelve experiment methods

Product School’s experimentation playbook [7] covers split tests, multivariate tests, demand probes, landing pages, usability prototypes, manual simulations, staged rollouts and adaptive personalisation. The catalogue below adds technical and operational tests, with recommended evidence limits for each.

Experiment catalogue for business and technical discovery
MethodQuestion and signalLimits and technical follow-up
Fake-door or smoke testQuestion and signalDoes an early-access offer attract interest? Compare eligible exposures with selections or requests to participate.Limits and technical follow-upExplain availability when users select the offer. Interest does not establish sustained value, willingness to pay or build feasibility. Avoid implying that a consequential action has completed.
Landing page or message testQuestion and signalWhich value proposition attracts the intended audience? Record qualified visits, enquiries and sign-ups.Limits and technical follow-upRecord the audience and acquisition channel. Recruitment bias or different traffic can explain changes; use controlled allocation when claiming one message outperforms another.
Prototype and task-based usability testQuestion and signalCan users complete the intended task? Observe comprehension, errors, completion, assistance and recovery.Limits and technical follow-upA small qualitative study can reveal friction, but cannot estimate improvement across the user population. Note simulated behaviour and untested access needs.
Concierge testQuestion and signalDoes a service help when people deliver it openly? Observe outcomes, repeat use and the effort required to provide support.Limits and technical follow-upRecord manual effort and cost. Treat this as a test of service value; separately establish whether automation can reproduce the useful result.
Wizard of Oz test
Method guidance [12]		Question and signalHow do users interact with an apparently automated interface whose responses are supplied by a person? Observe expectations and task behaviour.Limits and technical follow-upAgree the participant briefing and debriefing in the research plan. Keep operator responses within plausible system limits; a skilled human’s output does not validate a model or integration.
Technical spike or proof of conceptQuestion and signalCan a critical capability or integration work under specified conditions? Run an executable check and measure the relevant limits.Limits and technical follow-upTest the real dependency where permitted. Record mocks, environment differences, test data, versions, failure cases and reproducible results. It does not establish demand.
Offline AI evaluationQuestion and signalCan the model or agent meet the agreed task criteria? Compare the AI with a simpler approach on cases kept separate from development and tuning.Limits and technical follow-upRecord model, prompts, data, retrieval and tool versions. Repeat variable behaviours and inspect failure cases. Offline quality does not establish adoption or production safety.
Proof-of-value pilotQuestion and signalDoes the concept improve a real workflow for a bounded group? Track task outcomes, repeat use and total service cost.Limits and technical follow-upUse a credible baseline or comparator and record selection effects. Include support and correction effort; plan deeper evaluation if the pilot cannot isolate the cause of improvement.
A/B or split test
Design guidance [13]		Question and signalDoes a defined change improve a chosen outcome? Randomly allocate eligible units to control and treatment, then estimate the difference.Limits and technical follow-upConfirm instrumentation, allocation unit, adequate sample and a planned stopping rule. Check guardrails and uncertainty; a small statistically detectable change may still have little practical value.
Multivariate test
Method guidance [14]		Question and signalWhich combination of factors works, and do they interact? Compare planned combinations, such as content and layout variants.Limits and technical follow-upPlan enough observations for the combinations. Use a simpler experiment when traffic is limited; changing several elements without a designed comparison obscures their effects.
Canary or beta rolloutQuestion and signalHow does an implemented change behave under limited exposure? Observe reliability, task outcomes, support demand and recovery.Limits and technical follow-upApply the release checks and stop criteria. Rollout monitoring alone is not a causal comparison. Keep an explicit control design when testing an improvement claim.
Adaptive personalisationQuestion and signalDoes a changing allocation policy improve outcomes across relevant users? Evaluate the policy and important segments over time.Limits and technical follow-upUse a comparison and analysis suited to adaptive allocation, with specialist input. Set exploration limits and guardrails; automatic adaptation alone does not demonstrate benefit.

The catalogue is working guidance for this lifecycle. [12] explains human-controlled prototypes; [13] supports controlled-test design; [14] explains multivariate combinations. Technical spikes and AI evaluations extend the earlier feasibility guidance.

Agree how to run and close the experiment

Before testing, the experiment owner agrees these arrangements with the relevant data, security and research specialists. Resolve unclear permissions before proceeding, or choose a safer test.

  • Permitted data: identify what may be collected, entered into AI tools, stored and shared. Use synthetic or appropriately de-identified data where possible; record retention and deletion arrangements.
  • Approved tools: confirm that the tools, models and hosting are approved for the intended data and use, including how providers handle submitted information.
  • Participant information: explain the purpose, prototype limitations, AI involvement, what will be recorded and how findings will be used. Confirm consent or other applicable participation requirements and a way to withdraw or report concerns.
  • Access restrictions: define who can use the prototype, access its data or invoke connected systems. Isolate the experiment, limit permissions and agree stop conditions for unexpected effects.
  • After the experiment: name the prototype owner and expiry date. Decide how code, data and credentials will be deleted, archived or reviewed for reuse. Any promotion to production follows the applicable implementation and release checks.
Fictional service-desk example 3 of 6: design the experiment

Draft PRD v0.1: staff request a draft, inspect permitted source citations, correct the response and send it themselves. The draft records these hypothesised states and the initial permission constraints before testing.

Experiment X-1: eight service-desk staff each attempt one routine guidance task per workflow, using tasks of similar difficulty. Half try the prototype first; half try the current workflow first. Record correctness without help, elapsed time including review and correction, retrieval failures and requests for assistance. Report results for all eight attempts per workflow, including unsuccessful attempts. Record current-workflow results again under these conditions; matching task difficulty and varying order reduce, but do not remove, learning effects and task differences.

Pre-agreed rule: consider a bounded pilot only at median time ≤ 9 minutes, at least 7/8 correct without help and no restricted content in tested cases. A known access breach stops the session for investigation. A small convenience sample is exploratory, not a statistically reliable effect estimate.

Use approved sandbox tools and synthetic tickets and test articles with different access permissions. Include denied and missing sources, misleading instructions inside retrieved content and keyboard-only use. Set a two-week learning budget, inform participants, record applicable consent and retention arrangements, and name the prototype owner and expiry date.

Follow the example: 4 of 6.

Output: Experiment record: question, method, participants or data, version, decision rule, budget and safety checks. Next: Build only enough to run this test in step 4.

4. Prototype and learn

Run the agreed experiment, observe the complete task and record what happened before interpreting it. Preserve the prototype, dataset and plan versions so results remain understandable. Check AI-generated prototypes against the design system, accessibility expectations and technical constraints before involving users.

Test realistic workflows across screens, roles and systems, including waiting, missing information, interruption and recovery. Include relevant experience levels and access needs. Record whose needs the sample does not cover; participant counts alone do not establish adequate evidence.

Record who owns the prototype, when it expires and what happens to it afterwards. Before reusing it in production, apply the implementation assurance checks. Include human review and correction time in the results.

Learn and revise the draft PRD in the same cycle

Link observations to source notes, separate observation from interpretation and retain contradictory evidence. Use findings to change the draft PRD, interaction states and assumptions together. Preserve the original decision rule; agree any revised criteria before the next test.

Generated personas, synthetic interviews and model critiques can suggest research questions. They are not observations of real users; see Nielsen Norman Group’s assessment of synthetic users [16]. Keep participant information in controlled records and link only the evidence needed for the decision.

Generate alternatives from verified findings

After a test, use the reviewed findings to generate different responses to the same need. Keep the original observations and test criteria alongside each proposed change. Compare alternatives by the failure they address, the value assumption they test and the technical work they require.

Include a simpler or non-AI approach where useful. Engineering checks whether the new behaviour remains feasible, and Design checks the complete journey. Select the smallest useful follow-up experiment; more generated variants are useful only when they expose a choice worth testing.

Test with the people who will use it

The Defence Product Playbook groups fast learning into four habits, which it calls TEST:

  • Trial with real operators: test with the people who will use the product, not project team members standing in for them.
  • Expose the riskiest assumption: build the least you can to test the assumption most likely to sink the product, then discard it.
  • Shorten the loop: measure the time from user feedback to a changed prototype in days. If the loop is slow, fix that first.
  • Turn tests into decisions: end each test by keeping, changing or dropping the idea.
Fictional service-desk example 4 of 6: prototype, learn and improve

X-1 result / draft PRD v0.2: current-workflow median is again 12 minutes. Prototype v0.1 reaches 10 minutes, but only 6/8 staff complete correctly without help. No restricted content is observed. Two staff cannot recover when a source is missing; the pre-agreed rule is not met.

Rework: improve. Keep the proposal provisional. Make sources easier to see and show staff how to take over when a source is missing. Plan X-2 within the remaining budget. Draft PRD v0.3 adds R-1: cite permitted sources or explain why no draft is available. Earlier findings and criteria stay linked.

X-2 result / prototype v0.2: the same eight staff each attempt one new matched task per workflow, again varying which workflow they try first. The current-workflow median remains 12 minutes; the prototype achieves 8/8 correct without help and a median of 8.5 minutes, including review and correction. Access tests reveal no restricted content. Repeat participation, prior prototype feedback and limited task coverage constrain the conclusion; a wider pilot is still needed.

Follow the example: 5 of 6.

Output: Versioned prototype, observations, result and limitations; revised draft PRD and next-risk list. Next: Compare evidence with the original rule in step 5.

5. Evaluate and decide

Product, Design and Engineering compare the findings and limitations with the agreed decision rule. Review user value, feasibility, cost, strategic fit and guardrails together. The authorised decision owner records what happens next. Reviews inform that decision; approval follows local authority.

Choose one recorded outcome for the next cycle
DecisionEvidence and next move
CommitEvidence supports a defined scope, with acceptable limits and owners for unresolved questions. Prepare handoff in step 6.
Continue testingEvidence is missing or inconclusive, and does not yet justify changing the proposal. Return to step 3 with a specific question and remaining budget.
Rework: improveEvidence supports the idea, but the prototype needs improvement. Return to step 4, updating the experiment plan if needed.
Rework: redesignThe problem remains credible but the solution is weak. Return to alternatives in step 2.
Rework: pivotThe intended user, problem or expected value changes. Return to problem framing in step 1.
DeferA temporary dependency blocks useful learning. Record its owner and a review date or reopening trigger; no implementation is authorised.
StopNo justified case remains, risk is unacceptable, or the learning budget is exhausted without support for further investment. Archive the learning and close access safely.

Check risk and budget on every loop. A harmful or prohibited experiment stops for investigation; any resumed test needs a permitted design. Neither a favourable average score nor a commitment decision waives applicable controls.

Keep investigation, implementation and release decisions distinct

Evidence for investigation, implementation and production decisions
DecisionEvidence to review
Worth investigatingA credible problem, obligation or foreseeable risk; the consequence of doing nothing; a material uncertainty; and a bounded, permitted research or experiment plan with an owner and budget.
Worth a bounded implementationEvidence supporting the chosen problem and solution under recorded conditions; feasible scope, acceptance criteria, expected value, cost and constraints; and owners for remaining uncertainties and risks.
Safe for productionEvidence from the implemented product against applicable release criteria: security, privacy, accessibility, reliability, operational readiness, monitoring and recovery, with residual risks reviewed by the authorised decision makers. Prototype results alone do not establish this.

Resolve assumptions that could invalidate the solution, or narrow the scope, before committing to implementation.

Keep reviews light and regular

Review findings when they could change the next decision. Invite other teams when the proposal affects their services or shared patterns. Two useful review formats are:

  • Focused design review: Product, Design and Engineering examine the prototype, user evidence, accessibility, design-system patterns and feasibility. Record changes and unresolved questions.
  • Cross-team review: invite people who own affected services, domain rules, shared components or controls. Ask for specific feedback on dependencies and inconsistencies. Size participation to the decision; collect input asynchronously where practical.

The decision owner records which feedback changes the proposal and why. Ask:

  1. What uncertainty did we address?
  2. What did the evidence change?
  3. What is now the highest-risk assumption?
  4. What can we now decide?

Check how the concept has changed

Before investing more, compare the proposal with the concept brief. Record changes and the evidence behind them:

  • Intent and evidence: changes to the user, problem, outcome or solution, and the findings that explain them.
  • Scope and risk: additions, removals, dependencies and changes to permissions, controls or expected value.
  • Effort and cost: updated estimates from Engineering and other relevant contributors, including ranges, assumptions and uncertainty.
  • Decision: whether the next investment remains justified, who decides and what still needs testing.

Update the brief and PRD with agreed changes. Keep earlier criteria and results so reviewers can follow the decision.

Keep human approval where the consequences exceed the organisation’s risk tolerance. Examples include material regulatory interpretation, irreversible commitments to users, security exceptions, high-impact automated actions, costly architecture decisions and deployment into sensitive domains. Widen agent autonomy only when permissions, evaluation coverage, monitoring, known failure modes and rollback make the remaining risk acceptable.

Fictional service-desk example 5 of 6: evaluate and decide

Decision D-1: X-1 justified improvement, not commitment. X-2 now meets the exploratory rule: 12 → 8.5 minutes (target ≤ 9), 8/8 correct (target ≥ 7/8), and no restricted content observed in the tested cases. The designated decision owner commits to implementing a bounded pilot for routine guidance.

Technical evidence F-1: the read-only retrieval interface returns permitted sources and withholds denied content in the sandbox tests. Response times meet the pilot’s recorded limit at the tested load. Engineering records versions, missing-source behaviour and differences from production.

Cost evidence C-1: estimated implementation, hosting, review and support costs fall within the agreed pilot budget. The estimate records ranges, and the service owner confirms support capacity. Broader scale and lifetime cost remain open questions.

The record links X-1/X-2, F-1, C-1, alternatives considered, remaining risk and the rationale. It excludes access grants, request submission and autonomous sending. Product and Design own the wider pilot and research coverage; Engineering owns scale and integration questions. This is not a production release decision.

Follow the example: 6 of 6.

Output: Dated decision, evidence links, rationale, scope changes, owners and next actions. Next: Only commit advances to step 6; use the named return step for other outcomes.

6. Prepare the handoff

After the decision to implement, record the PRD version and link its scope to the experiments, decision and UI or API examples. Include acceptance criteria, exclusions, constraints and owners for open questions. Record what happens to prototype code, data and credentials. Product, Design and Engineering stay involved when implementation findings challenge the requirements.

Validation handover package
ArtefactContent to carry forwardReadiness check
Opportunity and decisionContent to carry forwardProblem, users, outcome, baseline, alternatives, selected concept and reasons; the next investment, decision owner and date.Readiness checkThe recommendation follows from the evidence, including conflicting findings and rejected options.
PRD and experienceContent to carry forwardBounded scope, exclusions, stories, acceptance criteria, quality targets and UI artefacts or representative API interactions.Readiness checkThe intended behaviour is testable, including failure, permission, recovery and accessibility cases.
Validation evidenceContent to carry forwardAssumptions, test criteria, method, participants or datasets, versions, results, limitations and evidence links.Readiness checkSupported, unsupported and inconclusive claims are distinct; tests cover the highest-risk business and technical assumptions.
Technical findingsContent to carry forwardSystem and data-flow context, approach options, spike results, dependency confirmations, initial architecture decisions and build/run cost ranges.Readiness checkEngineering can explain why the bounded scope appears feasible and which conditions limit that conclusion.
Remaining uncertaintyContent to carry forwardRisk or unknown, potential impact, owner, next check, time or cost bound, and trigger to reconsider scope or stop.Readiness checkBlocking unknowns return to discovery. Any accepted uncertainty has an explicit resolution and escalation route.
Delivery and measurementContent to carry forwardThe first useful slice, outcome and guardrail measures, telemetry and evaluation needs, and production evidence still required.Readiness checkThe delivery team can plan the TRD and tasks, collect missing evidence and identify when to reopen discovery.

For AI-assisted findings that affect a decision, retain the checked source extract, model or tool version, instructions and reviewer. Link the finding to the decision and restrict access as needed. Label generated scenarios and discarded interpretations so delivery can distinguish them from user evidence.

Fictional service-desk example 6 of 6: prepare the handoff

Evidence-backed PRD v1.0: routine guidance only, linked to P-1, concept brief v0.1, X-1/X-2 and decision D-1. Evidence item E-2 in Figure 7 summarises X-2. R-1 requires permitted citations or explicit handback. UI-3 shows missing or denied sources without a draft. Acceptance criterion AC-1 expects no returned content when source access is denied. Test case T-ACL-03 passes on prototype v0.2; repeat it on the implemented system.

The handoff includes interaction states, the read-only retrieval contract, F-1’s technical findings, C-1’s cost ranges, permission assumptions, the plan for closing the prototype, the wider-pilot plan and owned questions about scale, running cost and task coverage. The exploratory user results and supporting technical and cost evidence justify the next investment under the recorded conditions; they do not establish long-term value or production safety.

Return to the problem evidence.

For products using agents at runtime, include the tested limits on actions, approval points, failure and recovery cases, and evaluation results. Link each to intended behaviour and acceptance criteria.

Use the shared handoff package and implementation readiness checks for the full checklist. Implementation covers technical design, task slicing, verification and release; those procedures are not repeated here.

If implementation uncovers a bounded defect, correct it in that loop. If evidence challenges the user, problem, value or intended behaviour, return to the appropriate discovery step and record the change. Feedback does not automatically authorise model retraining or wider permissions.

Output: Versioned evidence-backed PRD and linked artefacts, with remaining risks and questions assigned. Next: Continue to implementation readiness; release requires evidence from the implemented product.

Optional deep dives

The six steps above are the main path. Open these references when the product or learning question calls for them; they do not add mandatory stages.

Reference: discovery frameworks

Choose a framework for the question

A framework organises discovery work; a method gathers evidence about a particular question. Use the six steps above as the shared process, and choose frameworks within them. Product School’s discovery guide [6] introduces six useful approaches: dual-track discovery and delivery, Jobs To Be Done, Double Diamond, Design Sprint, Lean Startup and Opportunity Solution Trees.

The table shows where each approach helps and the working artefact to retain. Use the originating sources for each framework; the JTBD row also links the Christensen Institute’s account [18]. Suggested records and technical checks are this guide’s recommendations: no framework removes the need to investigate feasibility or review the evidence.

Discovery frameworks and how to apply them
FrameworkUse and working artefactTechnical discovery connection
Continuous discovery and delivery
SVPG [10]		Use and working artefactUse when learning continues alongside implementation. The same Product, Design and Engineering contributors investigate upcoming options while delivery develops bounded, supported scope. Keep a shared learning backlog and decision record. Cagan’s article now favours continuous discovery and delivery over its older “Dual-track Agile” label, to emphasise principles rather than process.Technical discovery connectionRoute integration, operating-cost and quality findings back into discovery. Keep collaboration active through handover; separate workstreams do not require separate teams.
Jobs To Be Done
Christensen Institute [18]		Use and working artefactUse when the underlying need is unclear. Investigate the circumstances, the progress users seek, its functional, social and emotional dimensions, and why current alternatives fall short. Retain an evidence-linked job statement.Technical discovery connectionExplore constraints in the user’s actual setting, including access, devices, connectivity and workarounds. Keep the desired outcome independent of a preferred technology.
Double Diamond
Design Council [2]		Use and working artefactUse when the team is converging too early. Discover and Define expand and narrow the problem; Develop and Deliver explore and test responses. Retain problem and concept alternatives with reasons for narrowing them.Technical discovery connectionExplore reuse, process changes and different technical approaches before commitment. See the Double Diamond explanation.
Design Sprint
GV [11]		Use and working artefactUse for a focused question with available participants and decision makers. The five-day format maps the challenge, sketches options, chooses a direction, prototypes and tests it. Retain the storyboard, prototype and observations.Technical discovery connectionInvolve Engineering in choosing the testable slice. Run a separate spike for simulated integrations; the sprint’s prototype findings do not settle implementation feasibility.
Lean Startup
Build–Measure–Learn [9]		Use and working artefactUse repeated learning cycles when the value proposition or operating model is uncertain. Choose an assumption, build the smallest credible test, measure the result and decide whether to persevere or change direction. Retain the hypothesis, measures and decision.Technical discovery connectionInclude build, run and support cost in the learning. A minimum viable product (MVP) used by real users still needs the controls appropriate to its data, actions and exposure.
Opportunity Solution Tree
Teresa Torres [8]		Use and working artefactUse to connect a desired outcome to researched user opportunities, alternative solutions and assumption tests. Retain the tree and links to evidence; compare several responses to the selected opportunity.Technical discovery connectionAttach feasibility assumptions and spike results to solution branches. Keep user opportunities distinct from implementation tasks or a list of requested features.

Combine only the practices the decision needs

For example, use JTBD interviews to understand a task, an Opportunity Solution Tree to compare responses, and a focused sprint to test an interaction. Use Build–Measure–Learn to repeat the experiments and continuous discovery to keep learning connected to delivery. Record the question, evidence and next decision rather than treating framework completion as progress.

When agents use the product: test their journey

Test the experience when an agent acts for a user

When the product will be operated by AI agents, test that interaction during discovery. Sumit Sheth calls this agentic user experience (AUX): designing how agents use a product alongside its human experience. Exposing an API alone does not establish a useful journey.

The following are suggested discovery checks for such products. For software that only uses AI during development, continue with the usual user and service journeys.

Suggested checks for a journey carried out by an agent
Part of the journeyWhat to test
Intent and contextCan the agent identify the intended task, obtain permitted context and ask for missing information without inventing it?
Permission and controlCan the user see the proposed action, set its scope, give any required approval and stop further work?
Action and resultCan the agent choose the appropriate operation and distinguish a completed task from a request that was merely accepted?
Failure and recoveryWhat happens after a timeout, partial completion, ambiguous instruction or denied access? Check that a retry does not duplicate a consequential action.
Explanation and handbackCan the user inspect what changed, correct the result, recover where possible and take over with enough context?

Example · fictional agent journey

For an assistant that submits access requests, test a sandbox journey with missing details, approval refused and a timeout after submission. Observe whether it asks for clarification, respects the refusal and checks request status before retrying. Record task correctness, duplicate requests and the effort needed to take over.

Record the model, tool interface, permissions and test conditions with the prototype version. Repeat variable behaviours and inspect the resulting system state. Use the AI evaluation guidance to plan deeper checks during implementation.

Inspiration: [5] on AUX. The checks and example above are this guide’s recommendations.

Advanced: link intent, decisions and requirements

Product intent explains why a product exists, what it should do and which limits apply. Keep the evidence, requirements, designs, decisions and open questions linked. Review contradictions before using these records as context for an agent.

Link the intended outcomes to product behaviour and the architecture that supports it. Show how policy and evaluation apply across those links:

  • a product behaviour exists because it supports a user and business outcome;
  • an architecture choice exists because it enables required behaviour under known constraints;
  • a policy control exists because it addresses a defined risk; and
  • an evaluation shows whether the intended behaviour and constraints are met.

Keep product intent versioned, owned, accessible and auditable. Where practical, make the most valuable parts machine-readable: API descriptions, schemas, policy rules, acceptance tests and evaluation datasets can be checked automatically, not only read.

Record feedback and decisions between meetings

Attach feedback to a specific version of the brief, prototype or PRD. State the question, response deadline and decision owner. Keep one linked decision record with the date, options considered, evidence, rationale, actions and superseded decisions.

Link relevant comments and discussion notes from that record. Check AI-generated summaries against the original notes before relying on them, and confirm material decisions with their owners. Use recordings only where permitted, with agreed access and retention.

A useful specification makes assumptions, constraints, permissions, non-functional requirements, edge cases and exclusions explicit. Increase precision as uncertainty falls, and revise intent when evidence changes. Read about spec-driven development. GitHub Spec Kit’s methodology [4] advocates versioned specifications, linked technical plans and feedback from implementation; treat this as a proposed method and verify generated code against the requirements.

Advanced: connect measures to value

Draw on several kinds of evidence

  • User evidence: interviews, usability studies, support cases and co-creation sessions.
  • Behavioural evidence: product analytics, controlled experiments, workflow completion and adoption.
  • Operational evidence: telemetry, reliability, latency, incidents, model traces and recovery.
  • Evaluation evidence: offline datasets, automated tests, agent evaluations, policy checks and calibrated model-based judges.
  • Cost evidence: experiment cost, delivery effort, inference cost and the human attention consumed.

Use AI summaries to find themes worth checking against the original feedback. A summary does not establish cause, and an evaluation score covers only the cases and criteria used. Read how to evaluate AI behaviour and check model-based judgements.

Link each result to its research notes, dataset or test run. Keep participant information in the appropriate controlled location and summarise only what the decision needs. When evidence conflicts, record the conflict rather than averaging it into a reassuring conclusion.

Product, Design and Engineering should review feedback from use together. If evidence challenges the user need or intended behaviour, reopen discovery; if it reveals a bounded implementation defect, route it to delivery. Change the product intent through a recorded decision; feedback does not automatically authorise model retraining or broader agent permissions.

Connect the measures chosen in Frame

Features shipped, prototypes generated, prompts submitted and lines of AI-generated code measure activity. They do not show user impact or business value. Define measures at each of these layers:

Suggested measurement layers; set local measures and thresholds before testing
LayerWhat it answers
User outcomeDid the user achieve the outcome that makes the product worthwhile?
Business outcomeDid the product create the intended value for the organisation?
Product behaviourDid users adopt the behaviour that should drive the outcome?
Leading indicatorsAre early signals moving in the expected direction?
Learning speed and costHow quickly and affordably did a hypothesis become credible evidence and a decision?
GuardrailsDid quality, safety, reliability, cost, privacy and fairness stay within tolerance?

Choose a value measure to steer by

Use the Defence Product Playbook’s four-rung ladder to connect resources and early signals to value and longer-term outcomes. This guide adapts the categories: the playbook calls logins, uptime and shipped features inputs; here, inputs mean resources invested. The table omits the source’s illustrative confidence percentages because it gives no calibration method.

The metric ladder, adapted from the Defence Product Playbook
RungWhat it shows
1. Input measureResources invested, such as team effort, funding or compute
2. Leading indicatorAn early behaviour change that supports part of the theory of change
3. Value measureThe intended outcome of solving the problem; the measure the team steers by
4. Outcome measureThe effect the organisation ultimately seeks; often slower to change than measures used to guide weekly work

Higher rungs aim to measure effects closer to the intended value, but confidence still depends on evidence quality and the causal link between measures. The playbook recommends one value measure per problem that can move at least twice a year. Explain how improving it contributes to the outcome above it, and test that relationship.

Uptime is an operational reliability measure. Depending on the product, it may be a guardrail, a service outcome or a direct contributor to mission value. Usage can be a leading indicator when evidence links it to the intended outcome. Neither is naturally a resource input, and neither alone demonstrates that the problem is being solved.

Ask whether the measure could improve while the intended outcome stays unchanged. Check the link between them. Keep useful operational measures and, unlike the playbook, consider self-reported outcomes such as satisfaction, effort and trust. Compare these with observed behaviour and service data, noting sampling and response biases. Check that measures are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound (SMART).

The playbook’s value-cost ratio measures outcome delivered per annual cost and tracks change year on year. State the outcome units, costs included and measurement period. Compare ratios only when those units and cost boundaries are comparable, or a justified common valuation makes comparison possible. Financial return on investment (ROI) also needs justified monetary benefits and costs.

When measured value plateaus, investigate whether the product is sustaining an essential outcome or meeting an obligation before shifting investment. Maintenance may preserve mission value, supportability and risk controls even when the headline measure no longer rises.

Measures worth considering include:

  • Time to validated learning: elapsed time from an explicit hypothesis to credible evidence and a decision.
  • Cost per experiment: the cost of producing credible learning, including compute and human review.
  • Human attention ratio: the share of team time spent on users, strategy, judgement, difficult exceptions and learning, rather than producing documents and coordinating.
  • Product guardrails: task success, correction and escalation rates, model errors, latency, reliability, cost, privacy and safety incidents, fairness where material, and user trust.

Measurement source: Defence Product Playbook [1], “Define the problem, measure the value”. The measurement adaptations and suggested learning measures are this guide’s recommendations, not organisational policy or standardised metrics.
